source.title: Aligned Data Can Induce Misalignment via Context Confusion
source.authors: Yavuz Faruk Bakman; D. Yaldiz; Baris Askin; Swastik Roy; Morteza Ziyadi; Salman Avestimehr; Sai Praneeth Karimireddy

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports context-specific misalignment after fine-tuning on aligned data, but explicitly distinguishes this from jailbreak-safety work. It does not test refusal of harmful requests, first-token KL concentration, bypasses, safety-localized weights, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The measured outcome is domain-specific misalignment on fairness, privacy, and physical-safety evaluations, not refusal rates or compliance with harmful user requests. The paper also discusses related benign-fine-tuning jailbreak-safety studies, but those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes four instruction-tuned models on data that is aligned in its own context. It measures judge-scored misalignment on benign queries in other domains (gender equality, privacy, physical safety). It does not measure compliance with harmful requests or refusal. It explicitly separates itself from jailbreak-safety work such as Qi et al. Its cross-domain benchmarks (XSTest safe subset, WildJailbreak adversarial benign subset) are benign prompts scored for misalignment, not harmful-request compliance. This is a related but different construct, so it does not test V2 or any other version. Benign fine-tuning eroding refusals is only discussed, in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that training on contextually aligned data can transfer behavior to contexts where it is misaligned ('context confusion'). This misalignment is narrow and evades general alignment evaluations. Generic safety data does not fix it, while evaluation-domain examples (in training or in context) do. They give a mechanism: similar query representations undergo similar fine-tuning shifts, supported by a causal intervention. They argue that inspecting training data alone cannot predict post-training alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies context-specific misalignment from aligned-data fine-tuning, not the original harmful fine-tuning or first-token-depth methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Misalignment outcomes vary by training/evaluation domain and model. Paraphrasing reduces the effect in some settings but does not eliminate it; the effect of a context-awareness prefix is mixed. Added evaluation-domain examples and aligned in-context examples mitigate it, while general safety-alignment data does not reliably do so.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on contextually aligned data raised misalignment on matched evaluation domains. Gender equality went from 0.6–3.4% to 29.2–51.1%; privacy from 0.2–2.4% to 11.9–31.2%. There was little rise cross-domain or on XSTest-safe, WildJailbreak-benign or EM benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligned-data fine-tuning can transfer a learned behavior into a different context where that behavior is misaligned, narrowly rather than broadly.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing in general safety-alignment data did not reliably reduce context confusion. Evaluation-domain training examples (about 50) or aligned in-context examples largely removed it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mitigating context-specific misalignment requires examples from the vulnerable context; generic safety data is insufficient.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected comparison-and-selection Dolly samples raised group-fairness misalignment more than random Dolly samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selection behavior learned from real instruction data can transfer to fairness-sensitive decisions.

record.problems: Results use synthetic datasets and an LLM judge for coherency and misalignment scoring. The main text reports three-run means but no uncertainty estimates in the reported results. Several plotted results are not numerically specified in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct result rows were extracted for the paraphrase conditions, context-awareness prefix, layerwise feature localization, or representation-similarity analyses; these do not measure any of the listed claim versions, and plotted values are not stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples and no harmful-request compliance measured.
Benign or aligned fine-tuning is done, but harmful-request compliance and refusal rates are never measured; only domain misalignment on benign queries.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
Activation-space misalignment vectors are localized, but there is no test of safety-carrying weights or ranks.
The proposed mechanism (similar query representations shift similarly) concerns context confusion, not first-token shallowness.
No training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: The study is adjacent to V2 but measures judge-scored domain misalignment, not harmful compliance. The physical-safety domain scores dangerous advice to benign questions, not compliance with harmful requests. Results come from synthetic data and a GPT-based judge. No uncertainty is reported, though there is a threshold-robustness check (Appendix B.2).

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful requests or measure harmful-request refusal/compliance.
Fine-tunes on aligned context-specific data, but measures domain-specific misalignment rather than harmful-request compliance or refusal.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test.
Localizes behavioral features as activation-space vectors; does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Proposes a representational-transfer mechanism for context confusion, not a mechanism for first-token shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate safety behavior spread beyond initial response tokens.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B (range reported across models)
rows.operation_detail: SFT on aligned gender-based selection examples from animal breeding/husbandry
rows.measure: Misalignment rate on the corresponding evaluation domain
rows.note: The paper reports ranges across the four models rather than assigning every plotted value in the text.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B (range reported across models)
rows.operation_detail: SFT on aligned research-data retention and sharing examples
rows.measure: Misalignment rate on the corresponding evaluation domain
rows.note: The paper reports ranges across the four models rather than assigning every plotted value in the text.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: SFT on factual descriptions of risky or violent behavior in other contexts
rows.measure: Misalignment rate on the physical-safety evaluation
rows.baseline: Llama models already had relatively high base misalignment; exact baseline not stated in text
rows.value: Qwen models showed increases similar to the other domains; Llama models increased by up to 6.3 percentage points
rows.note: The text summarizes the Qwen results qualitatively and gives the maximum Llama increase; individual values are not stated there.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate matched and cross-domain pairs and broad alignment benchmarks after context-specific SFT
rows.value: Misalignment was primarily triggered in matched training/evaluation domains; the stated exception was Llama-3.2-3B privacy evaluation after safety training at 13%, below 31.2% in the matched privacy-training condition. No substantial increases were observed in remaining cross-domain settings and external benchmarks.
rows.note: The authors characterize the effect as narrow and context-specific.
rows.check: In the record, 'after safety training' means fine-tuning on the physical-safety-domain training set, not safety-alignment training. The exception is the cross-domain cell 'physical-safety training → privacy evaluation' at 13% for Llama-3.2-3B, versus 31.2% matched. No baseline is given. The row also merges several cross-domain cells and external benchmarks into one row.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Mix general safety-alignment examples into aligned context-specific training data

conditions.value: 500 to 4,000 PKUSafeRLHF-QA samples or 2,483-sample Bianchi et al. safety dataset

rows.baseline: Fine-tuning on research-domain data without added safety-alignment data; exact rate not stated in text
rows.value: Adding general safety-alignment data did not reliably reduce misalignment; rates remained high even when alignment data was four times larger than the training dataset, and the trend was non-monotonic.
rows.note: The stated outcome is an incomplete and non-reliable mitigation of context confusion.
rows.check: This row mixes general safety-alignment data (PKU-SafeRLHF, Bianchi) as an attempted mitigation of context confusion. It is not a measure of safety erosion or deepening, so no version link is correct. The state describes how well the mitigation worked, not a claim effect.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Add aligned examples from the evaluation domain to the original training data
rows.measure: Misalignment rate on held-out privacy evaluation examples
rows.baseline: Fine-tuning on the 1,000-sample original dataset without evaluation-domain examples; exact rate not stated in text
rows.value: As few as 50 aligned evaluation-domain examples substantially mitigated context confusion; the plotted results are described as reaching base-model rates with 50 samples.
rows.note: Evaluation samples were split into training and test subsets to avoid contamination.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Provide aligned in-context examples from the evaluation domain at inference
rows.baseline: Fine-tuned model without the in-context examples; exact rate not stated in text
rows.value: Aligned in-context examples nearly completely eliminated context confusion.
rows.note: The count was varied and different examples were used for each query.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune on selected comparison-and-selection examples from Dolly
rows.measure: Misalignment rate on group fairness questions
rows.baseline: Fine-tuning on randomly selected Dolly samples; exact rates not stated in text
rows.value: Fine-tuning on selected samples increased misalignment more than fine-tuning on random samples.
rows.note: The authors interpret the difference as transfer of selection behavior from aligned to misaligned contexts.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction and Section 5 discuss benign fine-tuning and jailbreak safety, explicitly distinguishing that literature from the study's context-confusion experiments.

tranche.reason: Measures context-specific behavioral misalignment on benign queries, a different construct from harmful-request compliance. Its representation analyses and mitigations do not test the other claim versions.

source_check.notes: In Section 3.2, safety training means training on the physical-safety-domain dataset. Several check-pack fields are ellipsized; checks cover their displayed content.
